samples.text:
In many countries, patients must wait for weeks or even months to get treatment in public hospitals. This is a serious problem because some illnesses become worse during this time. In this essay I will discuss the causes of this problem and suggest some solutions.

The main cause is that there are not enough doctors and nurses. In some countries, many medical staff leave public hospitals to work in private clinics or abroad, because the salary is higher. So the remaining staffs have too many patients to treat. Another cause is that the population is getting older. Old people often have more health problems, so they need to visit hospital more often, and this increase the number of patients. In addition, some public hospitals do not have enough money to buy modern equipment or build more rooms, so they cannot treat many patients at the same time. Finally, sometimes people go to hospital for small problems which a local doctor could treat.

There are several solutions to this problem. First, the government should spend more money on public health, to build new hospitals and buy equipment. Second, it is important to train more doctors and nurses and pay them better salary, so they want to stay in public hospitals. Also, the government can open more small clinics in local areas, so people with minor illness can go there instead of the hospital. This will reduce the pressure on big hospitals.

In conclusion, long waiting times are caused by a shortage of staff, an ageing population and lack of money. I think the government should invest more in health care and train more staff, because health is the most important thing for people.
samples.why: Causes and solutions both covered with relevant points · explanations brief and some ideas listed · clear but mechanical organisation · adequate vocabulary · errors with plurals, articles and agreement that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Long waiting lists have become a familiar feature of public healthcare in many countries, with patients sometimes waiting months for operations or specialist appointments. This essay will examine the main causes of these delays and propose several possible solutions.

One of the key causes is a shortage of medical staff. Training a doctor takes many years, and in some countries public hospitals struggle to keep qualified staff, who may be attracted by the higher salaries offered in private clinics or abroad. Demand for treatment, meanwhile, have risen steadily. Populations are ageing, and older people are more likely to suffer from long-term conditions that require regular care. A further cause is inefficient use of existing resources. In many systems, hospital beds are occupied by elderly patients who are well enough to leave but cannot be discharged because there is no suitable care available at home, which means fewer beds for new patients. Emergency departments are also overloaded by people with minor complaints that could be treated elsewhere.

To reduce waiting times, governments should first invest in the workforce by funding more training places and improving pay and conditions so that staff remain in the public sector. Secondly, strengthening primary care would ease the pressure on hospitals. If local clinics and pharmacies were better equipped to deal with minor illnesses, fewer patients would need hospital treatment. Improving social care is equally important, as it would allow patients who no longer need medical attention to leave hospital sooner and free up beds. Finally, hospitals could make better use of technology, such as online booking systems and remote consultations, to organise appointments more efficiently.

In conclusion, long waiting times result from staff shortages, rising demand and inefficient use of resources. Investment in staff, stronger primary and social care and smarter organisation could significantly shorten these delays.
samples.why: Clear position · causes explained with supporting detail, including bed shortages · solutions matched to causes · good collocation (primary care, free up beds) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
In many countries with publicly funded healthcare, lengthy waiting lists have become one of the most visible signs of a system under strain. Patients may wait months for diagnostic tests or surgery, sometimes seeing their condition deteriorate in the meantime. The causes are several and interrelated, and so are the solutions.

At the heart of the problem is a mismatch between rising demand and constrained capacity. Ageing populations mean that more people are living with chronic conditions requiring ongoing treatment, while advances in medicine have expanded the range of procedures that can be offered. Capacity, by contrast, has not kept pace. Medical staff take years to train, and public hospitals often lose experienced doctors and nurses to better-paid private practice or to other countries, leaving those who remain overstretched. Inefficiencies elsewhere in the system compound these shortages. When adequate social care is unavailable, patients who are medically fit to leave hospital occupy beds for days or weeks, creating bottlenecks that ripple back through wards and emergency departments. Similarly, weak primary care means that many conditions which could be managed in the community end up in hospital.

The most sustainable response is to expand and retain the workforce, which means increasing training places while improving pay, working conditions and career development in the public sector. Staffing alone will not suffice, however, unless patient flow is improved. Investing in social care would allow timely discharge, and strengthening local clinics would intercept minor complaints before they reach hospital. Hospitals can also increase throughput by separating planned surgery from emergency services, so that routine operations are not cancelled whenever emergency admissions surge. Digital scheduling and remote follow-up appointments offer further gains in efficiency.

In conclusion, long waits stem from rising demand, workforce shortages and bottlenecks elsewhere in the system. Addressing them requires sustained investment in staff alongside reforms that allow patients to move through care more smoothly.
samples.why: Causes and solutions fully addressed with a clear analytical frame (demand versus capacity) · logically sequenced, well-extended ideas · precise vocabulary (bottlenecks, throughput, patient flow) · wide range of accurate structures.
